summary: LUNEXIS is a web tool that lets mission planners, educators and the public compare candidate landing sites near the Moon's south pole. Pick up to three sites and a date range in 2027, and LUNEXIS shows how much of the time the Sun is above the horizon (solar power potential) and when Earth is in view (direct-to-Earth communication). Results appear as simple scores, a sky view that moves with time, and a color-coded timeline. It addresses the challenge by replacing complicated tools with one clear, fast interface, so people can judge a site's lighting and communication conditions in seconds.
details:
LUNEXIS is an interactive tool for comparing sunlight availability and Earth visibility at four approximate lunar south-pole sites: Shackleton, Malapert Massif, Haworth, and Faustini. It uses NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE kernels with the Skyfield library to calculate hourly apparent Sun and Earth positions throughout 2027. Users can select sites and dates, explore sky positions over time, and compare visibility summaries on a timeline.

The project makes orbital and lunar-orientation data easier to explore for early mission planning and education. It is a research visualization, not a navigation product: the sites are approximate, the horizon is modeled as flat, and terrain is not included. The team considered visibility thresholds, time coverage, usability, and communicating these limitations.

The site uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Data processing uses Python, Skyfield, and NumPy. No special hardware was used.
